Header: Cholesterol crystal embolism–associated acute kidney injury (CCE-AKI) is characterized by the obstruction of small arteries and arterioles by cholesterol crystals released from atherosclerotic plaques. These emboli induce endothelial injury, activation of the coagulation system (“crystal clot”), and immune cell infiltration, predominantly involving myeloid cells. Complement activation has been proposed as a key contributor to CCE-AKI pathophysiology, based primarily on in vitro and in vivo experimental models. Because vascular injury is central to CCE-AKI, small arteries represent a key compartment for investigating these processes. In the skin, cholesterol emboli are typically detected within arteries of the deep dermis rather than the superficial dermis, providing an additional tissue compartment in which to investigate vascular complement activation. Here, we present a representative artery from the papillary dermis of a patient with CCE-AKI.

Waypoints.Name: Artery
Waypoints.Description: In CCE-AKI, cholesterol crystals are typically detected in arteries located within the deep dermis. Here, the image shows a small artery from the papillary (superficial) dermis.

Waypoints.Name: Complement activation
Waypoints.Description: Complement activation is barely detectable in superficial arteries from this patient with CCE-AKI, with only C3 (detected using an anti-C3d antibody) and C9 deposits observed within the arterial wall.

Waypoints.Name: Immune infiltrate
Waypoints.Description: No immune cells are detected in the periarterial space.
